goals: Apply Naive Bayes to text classification
Know when it works well despite the assumption
why: Naive Bayes powered early spam filters and remains a strong, very fast baseline for text classification: support tickets, reviews, intent detection.
explain: Use **Bayes' theorem** to compute P(class | features). The "naive" part assumes features are **independent given the class**, so the likelihood becomes a simple product of per-feature probabilities.
In text, each word is a feature. P(spam | "free", "winner") ∝ P(spam) × P("free" | spam) × P("winner" | spam).
The independence assumption is obviously false (words co-occur), yet the **ranking** of classes is often right, so classification works well.
Variants: **Multinomial** (word counts), **Bernoulli** (word present/absent), **Gaussian** (continuous features). Use **Laplace smoothing** so that an unseen word does not zero out the whole product.

example.title: A two-word spam check
steps: Priors: P(spam) = 0.4, P(normal) = 0.6. Likelihoods: P(free | spam) = 0.30, P(free | normal) = 0.02; P(meeting | spam) = 0.05, P(meeting | normal) = 0.20
example.result: Predict spam with about 71% probability. "free" pushed strongly towards spam; "meeting" pulled it back towards normal. Each word multiplies in more evidence.

mistakes: Trusting its probabilities as calibrated: they tend to be extreme.

practice.code:
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer
from sklearn.naive_bayes import MultinomialNB
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
texts = ["free prize winner", "meeting at 10", "claim your free reward", "project update attached"]
labels = ["spam", "normal", "spam", "normal"]
m = make_pipeline(CountVectorizer(), MultinomialNB()).fit(texts, labels)
print(m.predict(["free meeting reward"]), m.predict_proba(["free meeting reward"]).round(2))

options: It assumes features are independent given the class
It only works for two classes
To avoid zero probabilities for unseen words
check.why: One zero would wipe out the whole product.

formula.tex: P(c \mid x_1, \dots, x_p) \propto P(c) \prod_{j=1}^{p} P(x_j \mid c)
formula.plain: The posterior for a class is proportional to its prior times one likelihood per feature, multiplied together.
